title: Sabbath at home
hookLine: some keep the Sabbath going to church; I keep it staying at home, with a bobolink
tomorrow: what can you give when you have nothing to give?

cards: Sunday morning: some people head to services, some to brunch, some to the couch with a twinge of guilt. Dickinson stayed home, and wrote it down.
"Some keep the Sabbath going to church; I keep it staying at home, With a bobolink for a chorister, And an orchard for a dome."

teach.b: Notice the verb: keep. She doesn't skip the Sabbath; she keeps it, in the garden. And for each piece of church she finds one outdoors.

teach.h: A BIRD CHOIR, AN ORCHARD DOME.
teach.b: A bobolink, a meadow songbird, sings in the choir. The orchard's branches make the dome. Instead of a surplice, she just wears her wings.
"God preaches, a noted clergyman, And the sermon is never long."
Then the last turn, which is the teaching: "So instead of getting to heaven at last, I'm going all along!" For Dickinson, the holy day isn't only a ticket for later.
Heaven isn't just where the road ends; it's the road, walked now, Sunday by Sunday, under the trees. Biographers say her family went to church and that she stopped going as an adult.
In this poem she doesn't call it leaving God.
She calls it keeping the day another way. The poem teases a little, the sermon is never long, but it calls no one wrong: some keep it this way, I keep it that way. Both are keeping.

how: Some people on this path keep one unhurried hour a week at home or outdoors as their own Sabbath: no tasks, a little reading, birdsong, or a walk.

o: Dickinson keeping the holy day in her own garden
a Sunday school class taught in a parlor
a family dinner Dickinson's father hosted weekly

s: Dickinson's poem says she gave up the Sabbath
she keeps it, staying at home.
in the poem, God preaches and the sermon is never long
the garden has its own preacher.
the poem says going to church is wrong
some keep it one way; she keeps it another.

games.q: a coworker says Sunday is her one day off and she feels lazy resting at home. what fits Dickinson's poem?
o: rest at home can be keeping a holy day, with what's around you.
rest only counts if you get something useful done.
Dickinson says every Sunday belongs in a church pew.
games.why: Dickinson kept the Sabbath, not skipped it: a bird for a choir, an orchard for a dome, heaven all along.

practice: Make this a small Sabbath, wherever you are. Close your eyes and let the room be the church: the hum of the house, a bird or a car outside, as the choir. Rest, with nothing to finish.
